criteria.descriptor: Full marks: every mechanism named is used correctly — a schema-defined network interface as source of truth, an appropriate sync-streaming/async pattern for long latency, correct HTTP/error semantics with retryable vs non-retryable distinction, idempotency keys for safe retries, provider-agnostic fields, and compatible versioning. Deduct for technical errors such as retrying non-idempotent 4xx, claiming a blocking call is fine at 30s, or conflating transport status with domain errors.

Full marks: covers all four asked dimensions — the interface mechanism, request/response+error shaping, an evolution/versioning strategy, and the LLM realities (latency, cost/billing, non-determinism) — plus at least some non-functional terms (auth, SLOs, rate/token limits). Partial credit as dimensions are missing; omitting error contract, versioning, or idempotency each drops a point.

Full marks: each major choice is justified by the scenario's constraints — e.g. streaming/async chosen because of 3-30s latency and cascading-timeout risk, idempotency chosen because calls are billed and retried, provider-agnostic fields chosen to preserve the component boundary and independent deploys. Lower marks for asserting choices without tying them to the decoupling/latency/cost pressures.

Full marks: a well-organized answer that a design-review audience could act on — clearly separates interface, payload/error shape, evolution, and LLM concerns, uses precise vocabulary (contract, idempotency, backward-compatible, SLO, tolerant reader), and reads as a coherent proposal rather than a scattered list. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-without-meaning writing.

expected_answer_points: Replace the shared module/DB with an explicit network interface governed by a single versioned schema (OpenAPI/protobuf/JSON Schema) as the source of truth, enabling independent deploys
Choose an interaction style suited to 3-30s latency: streaming (SSE/chunked) and/or async submit-and-poll (202 + job id) rather than a naive long blocking call, with explicit timeouts
Define a stable, typed error contract that separates transport errors from domain errors and distinguishes retryable (429/503/504) from non-retryable (400/422), carrying a request_id for tracing
Require idempotency keys so network retries of expensive, billed, non-deterministic calls do not double-generate or double-charge

Keep the contract provider-agnostic: hide vendor-specific params and the actual model choice behind stable fields so the generation team can swap models/providers without breaking the orchestrator (clean component boundary)
Evolve compatibly: additive-only changes, version bump for breaking changes, tolerant-reader behavior, and consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) enforced in CI
Include non-functional terms in the contract: auth (scoped token/mTLS), SLOs (latency/availability), rate limits, payload/token budgets, and usage/token counts returned for cost attribution
common_pitfalls: Describes only the happy-path request/response JSON and omits the error contract, versioning strategy, and non-functional terms — treating a data shape as if it were a full service contract
Proposes a single synchronous blocking call for a 3-30s generation with no streaming, async, or timeout strategy, ignoring cascading-timeout and held-connection risks
Conflates transport-level HTTP status with the domain error envelope, or recommends blanket retries that would retry non-retryable 4xx and double-generate/double-bill on a non-idempotent call
Bakes provider-specific fields or the concrete model name into the contract, leaking the implementation and recoupling the orchestrator to the generation team's internals
Keeps a shared library or shared database table (or introduces a shared schema-owning DB) as the 'contract,' which defeats independent deployability
Ignores versioning/compatibility, so any field change is a breaking change requiring a lock-step deploy — the exact problem the review is trying to fix — with no contract tests to catch drift
reference_answer:
Replace the shared module and table with an explicit network interface owned by a single versioned schema. I'd define an OpenAPI (or protobuf) spec as the source of truth and generate typed clients/stubs from it, so neither team reads the other's code or DB. That alone is the point of a service contract: it lets the two services deploy independently behind a stable boundary.

Interface and semantics: given 3-30s latency, a plain blocking request risks cascading timeouts and holds connections open, so I'd offer streaming (SSE / chunked responses) for the interactive path and/or an async submit-and-poll pattern (POST returns 202 + a job id, GET polls status) for batch. Requests carry only stable, provider-agnostic fields: assembled prompt or messages, max_tokens, a stop condition, a caller-supplied request_id, and an Idempotency-Key. The response carries the text (or stream), a finish_reason, token/usage counts for cost attribution, and the resolved model/version for observability. Crucially, vendor-specific knobs and the actual model choice stay hidden behind the contract so Team B can swap providers without breaking Team A — that is the component boundary.

Error contract: separate transport failures from a stable, typed domain-error envelope (e.g. code, message, retryable flag, request_id). Map to sane HTTP: 400/422 for bad input (non-retryable), 429/503 for rate-limit/overload (retryable with backoff), 504 for upstream timeout. Because retries on a non-idempotent, billed call would double-generate and double-charge, the Idempotency-Key lets the server dedupe.

Evolution: additive, backward-compatible changes only; breaking changes require a new version (URL or header) run side-by-side. Enforce with consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) in CI and a tolerant-reader posture (ignore unknown fields). Finally, bake non-functional terms into the contract: auth (scoped token/mTLS), latency and availability SLOs, rate limits, max payload/token budgets, and timeout expectations, so both teams share explicit, testable expectations.
